segs.text: Section ten. Target and mechanism of action. The fifth principle asks where in the body a compound acts and how it causes harm. The target can be a specific organ or a more general physiological endpoint. A compound can cause problems at more than one place, and not every place it hits may be known yet. If a compound damages the kidney and the liver, it likely damages them in different ways, because each target has its own mechanism.

The target organ may not be the site of highest concentration, because tissues differ in sensitivity. A compound can be most concentrated in muscle and cause no harm there, yet damage a more sensitive kidney at a lower concentration. She said, where it's having an adverse effect may not be where the highest concentration is, which is probably a little counterintuitive. Sensitivity still needs dose. The kidney has its own dose-response curve, so even a very sensitive organ is harmed only if the concentration reaching it is high enough.

The mechanism at each target may be different. That is why the effective, toxic and lethal curves of one drug are not parallel, and why many adverse effects on a drug's list have nothing to do with its therapeutic action. There are two kinds of side effect. Some are the therapy going too far at the intended target, such as a diuretic that removes too much fluid and leaves the patient needing hydration. Others come from a different target altogether. Aminoglycoside ototoxicity is her classic example of an adverse effect whose target is very different from the therapeutic one.

Her true or false items turn on the word always. The statement that a medication's concentration is always highest at its target site is false. The statement that a drug's mechanism of toxicity is always the same as its mechanism of efficacy is false. And a highly sensitive organ is not always damaged, because the dose at the target still decides.
